en: Sutta Nipāta 3.12 Dvayatānupassanāsutta Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.
Now on that occasion—the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, during the full moon night—the Blessed One was seated in the open air surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Then the Blessed One, having surveyed the silent Saṅgha of bhikkhus, addressed the bhikkhus:
“‘Bhikkhus, as to those wholesome states that are noble, leading out, and conducive to enlightenment— what, bhikkhus,
is the proximate cause for hearing those wholesome, noble, leading-out, and enlightenment-conducive states?
If, bhikkhus, they should ask you this, you should answer them thus:”
‘Only for the sake of knowing, as it really is, the nature of duality.
And what do you call this duality?
“This is suffering” and “this is the origin of suffering”—this is one contemplation.
“This is the cessation of suffering; this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering”—this is the second contemplation.
For a bhikkhu who dwells thus, correctly contemplating the two together, being heedful, ardent, and resolute, one of two fruits may be expected:
either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of a non-returner.
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:
“Those who do not understand suffering...”
Furthermore, the origin of suffering;
and where suffering ceases entirely and without remainder.
And they do not know that path leading to the stilling of suffering;
they are destitute of the liberation of mind.
And likewise for liberation through wisdom;
they are incapable of making an end,
for they truly go on to birth and old age.
Those who understand suffering,
as well as the origin of suffering,
and where suffering ceases entirely—
is ceased without remainder;
and they understand that path which leads to the stilling of suffering.
Those perfected in the liberation of mind,
and likewise in the liberation by wisdom,
are capable of making an end to suffering.
“They are not subject to birth, aging, or death.
“Bhikkhus, if those who ask were to say, ‘Could there be another way for the right contemplation of duality?
you should answer them, ‘There could be.’”
And how might this be?
"Whatever suffering arises, all of it has acquisition as its condition"—this is the first contemplation.
"But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of acquisitions, there is no arising of suffering"—this is the second contemplation.
Thus, with right [mindfulness]...
Then the Teacher further said this:
"Sufferings arise, having the acquisitions as their source."
Whatever various forms there are in the world, the fool who,
being ignorant, creates a substrate for existence,
undergoes suffering again and again.
"Therefore, one who understands should not create acquisitions,
observing that suffering originates from birth.
"Bhikkhus, if those who ask were to say, 'Could there be another way for the right contemplation of duality?'"
‘It may be so,’ it should be said. And how might it be so?
That whatever suffering arises, all of it has ignorance as its condition—this is one way of contemplation.
"But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is no arising of suffering"—this is the second contemplation.
Thus, right...
[as before] ...Then the Teacher spoke further as follows:
“Those who go again and again through the saṃsāra of birth and death,
from this state to another state— ”
Ignorance itself is that destination.
Ignorance is this great delusion,
by which this [cycle] has been spun out for so long.
And those beings who have attained true knowledge do not go to further existence.
"It might be by another way as well... [and so on].
And how might it be so?
"Whatever suffering arises, all of it has formations as its condition"—this is the first contemplation.
"But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of formations, there is no arising of suffering"—this is the second contemplation.
Thus, with right [mindfulness]...
Then the Teacher further said this:
"Whatever suffering arises,"
Everything has volitional formations as its condition;
with the cessation of volitional formations,
there is no arising of suffering.
Having understood this danger—
that suffering has conditioned phenomena as its cause—
one should seek the stilling of all conditioned phenomena.
Through the cessation of perceptions,
thus comes the destruction of suffering—
having known this as it truly is.
Those of perfect vision, masters of the Vedas,
wise through their thorough knowledge,
having overcome the fetter of Māra—

"Whatever suffering arises, all of it has consciousness as its condition"—this is the first contemplation.
"But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of consciousness, there is no arising of suffering"—this is the second contemplation.
Thus, correctly... [and so on].
Then the Teacher spoke further as follows:
"Whatever suffering arises,
all that is conditioned by consciousness."
With the cessation of consciousness,
there is no arising of suffering.
Having understood this danger,
Suffering has consciousness as its condition;
with the subsiding of consciousness, a bhikkhu is free from hunger and fully extinguished.
‘It might be by another way as well... And how might it be?
Whatever suffering arises, all that has contact as its condition—this is one contemplation.’
"But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of contact, there is no arising of suffering"—this is the second contemplation.
Thus, rightly...
[as before] ...then the Teacher further said this:
“For those who are beset by contact,
following the stream of existence,
having entered upon a wrong path,”
The destruction of the fetters is far away for those who,
having fully understood contact,
delight in final knowledge and tranquility.
"Indeed, through the full realization of contact, they are free from hunger and have attained final nibbāna.
"It might be by another way as well... [and so on].
And how might it be so?
"Whatever suffering arises, all of it has feeling as its condition"—this is the first contemplation.
"But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of feelings, there is no arising of suffering"—this is the second contemplation.
Thus, with right [mindfulness]...
Furthermore, the Teacher said this:
"Whether it be happiness or suffering,"
Together with that which is neither painful nor pleasant—
whatever is felt internally and externally.
Having known this as suffering—
deceptive by nature and subject to disintegration—
and seeing its passing away again and again,
Thus he understands therein:
"With the destruction of feelings,
the bhikkhu is free from hunger and has attained final nibbāna."
‘It may be by another way as well... And how might it be?
Whatever suffering arises, all that has craving as its condition—this is one contemplation.’
"But through the remainderless fading away and cessation of craving, there is no arising of suffering"—this is the second contemplation.
Thus, with right...
[as before] ...then further, the Teacher said this:
“With craving as his companion,
a person wanders through the long course of existence,
from this state of being to another state of being.”
One does not transcend saṃsāra.
Having understood this danger—
that craving is the origin of suffering—
Free from craving and without grasping, the mindful bhikkhu goes forth.
"It might be by another way as well... [and so on].
And how might it be so?
"Whatever suffering arises, all of it has clinging as its condition"—this is the first contemplation.
"But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of clinging, there is no arising of suffering"—this is the second contemplation.
Thus, with right [view]...
Furthermore, the Teacher said this:
"With clinging as condition, existence [comes to be]."
A being undergoes suffering;
for one who is born, there is death—
this is the origin of suffering.
Therefore, through the destruction of clinging,
by means of perfect knowledge, the wise,
having directly realized the destruction of birth, [attain Nibbāna].
They do not go to further existence.
"Could it be by another way as well... How might that be?"
"Whatever suffering arises, all of it has its condition in exertion"—this is the first contemplation.
"But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of exertions, there is no arising of suffering"—this is the second contemplation.
Thus, correctly... [and so on].
Then the Teacher spoke further as follows:
"Whatever suffering arises,
all of it is conditioned by exertion."
Through the cessation of undertakings,
there is no arising of suffering.
Having understood this danger,
Suffering arises from undertaking;
by relinquishing all undertakings,
one is liberated through non-undertaking.
For the bhikkhu whose craving for existence has been severed and whose mind is at peace,
the wandering through births is exhausted.
"There is no further becoming for him.
"Could it be by another way as well...? And how could that be?"
"Whatever suffering arises, all of it has nutriment as its condition"—this is the first contemplation.
"But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of nutriments, there is no arising of suffering"—this is the second contemplation.
Thus, correctly... [and so on].
Then the Teacher spoke further as follows:
“Whatever suffering arises,
all of it has nutriment as its condition.”
Through the cessation of nutriments,
there is no arising of suffering.
Having understood this danger,
Suffering arises with nutriment as its condition;
having fully understood all nutriment,
one is no longer dependent on any nutriment.
Having rightly understood health,
through the complete destruction of the taints,
one who dwells in the Dhamma, having reflected, frequents [the company] of those established in the Dhamma.
“The one who has realized the Vedas cannot be reckoned [by these means]. “Could it be by something else...?
And how could that be?”
"Whatever suffering arises, all of it has agitation as its condition"—this is the first contemplation.
"But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of agitations, there is no arising of suffering"—this is the second contemplation.
Thus, correctly... [etc.]
Then the Teacher spoke further as follows:
“Whatever suffering arises,
all of it is conditioned by agitation.”
With the cessation of the trembling,
there is no arising of suffering.
Having understood this danger,
Suffering arises conditioned by wavering;
therefore, having abandoned wavering and restrained the formations, [one should dwell].
“Unshaken and free from clinging,
the mindful bhikkhu wanders forth.
“It might be through something else…” [and so on].
And how might this be?
"For one who is dependent, there is wavering"—this is the first contemplation.
"One who is independent does not waver"—this is the second contemplation.
Thus, with right [view]...
Furthermore, the Teacher said this:
"One who is independent does not waver."
Dependent and grasping,
one does not transcend saṃsāra, with its state of being thus and its state of being otherwise.
Having understood this danger,
the great peril in dependencies,
one should be independent and without clinging.
“A mindful bhikkhu goes forth.
“Could it be by another way as well? … [as before] … “And how could it be so?”
"Monks, 'The formless is more peaceful than forms'—this is the first contemplation.
'Cessation is more peaceful than the formless'—this is the second contemplation.
Thus, correctly... [and so forth].
Then the Teacher spoke further as follows:
“Those beings who have reached the realm of form,
and those who abide in the formless realm;”
Not understanding cessation,
they return to renewed existence;
but those who have fully understood form—
Not settled in formless states,
those who are liberated in cessation—
those people are the destroyers of death.
‘It might be by another way as well... And how might it be?
That which, monks, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins—’

When, for the generation including devas and humans, that which is contemplated as "this is true" is seen with right wisdom as it really is as "this is false for the noble ones"—this is the first contemplation.

When, monks, for the generation including devas... including devas and humans, that which is contemplated as "this is false" is seen with right wisdom as it really is as "this is true for the noble ones"—this is the second contemplation.
Thus, with right [mindfulness]...
Then the Teacher further said this:
"Perceiving a self in what is not-self,"
Behold the world together with its devas,
settled upon name-and-form,
imagining "this is the truth."
For in whatever way they conceive it,
that thing becomes otherwise than that;
for that is a falsehood for them.
For that which is subject to deception is transient;
but Nibbāna is not subject to deception—
this the Noble Ones know in truth.
"Through the realization of these truths, they are free from hunger and have attained final nibbāna.
"Bhikkhus, if those who question you should ask: 'Could there be another way for the right contemplation of duality?'"
‘It may be,’ it should be said. And how might it be?
Whatever, monks, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, and among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins...

When that which has been contemplated by the world with its devas and humans as "this is happiness" is clearly seen as it really is with right wisdom by the noble ones as "this is suffering"—this is the first contemplation.

When, monks, that which has been contemplated by the world with its devas... [as above] ...and with its humans as "this is suffering" is clearly seen as it really is with right wisdom by the noble ones as "this is happiness"—this is the second contemplation.
“Monks, for a monk who dwells thus, correctly contemplating the two together, being heedful, ardent, and resolute, one of two fruits may be expected:
either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of a non-returner.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further spoke these words:
"Forms, sounds, tastes, smells, tangibles,
and mental objects in their entirety— "
Desirable, lovely, and pleasing—
so far as it is called "existence" (atthi) in this world together with its devas.
These things are considered happiness by you;
but that wherein they cease is considered suffering by them.
This peace, seen by the Noble Ones,
is the complete cessation of identity-view; it stands as an opposition to this [craving].
That which the whole world regards as happiness,
the Noble Ones regard as suffering.
That which others call suffering,
the noble ones know as happiness.
Behold this Dhamma, so difficult to understand!
The wise are not deluded here;
for those who are shrouded there is darkness,
a gloom for those who do not see.
The mind of the virtuous is open,
like light for those who see;
yet they do not perceive what is close at hand.
The deer who are skilled in the Dhamma [do not follow] those who have fallen under the sway of craving for existence and who drift along with the stream of existence.
This Dhamma is not easily awakened to by those who have entered the realm of Māra;
who indeed, other than the Maruts, [could understand it]?
One ought to awaken to that state, by fully understanding which,
the taintless ones attain final Nibbāna.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
And while this exposition was being spoken, the minds of about sixty bhikkhus were liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
The Twelfth Discourse on Contemplation of the Two:
Its Summary Verse Truth, acquisitions, and ignorance.
Volitional formations with consciousness as the fifth;
contact and craving as the factors to be felt;
clinging, undertaking, and nutriment.
"Form is subject to agitation and movement;
it is real by way of suffering in sixteen ways.
Thus ends the third chapter, the Mahāvagga.
Its summary verse:
Going forth, striving, and well-spoken words, O Sundarī.
The Māgha Sutta, Sabhiya,
Sela, and Salla are spoken;
and also Vāseṭṭha and Kokāli.
The Nālaka and the Dvayatānupassanā—
these twelve discourses are called the Mahāvagga.
